passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Welcome to the U.S. Bancorp Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. Following a review of the results, there will be a formal question-and-answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press star then 1 on your phone. If you wish to withdraw your question, please press star then 1 again. This call will be recorded and available for replay beginning today at approximately 10:00 a.m. Central time. I will now turn the conference call over to Brian Mauney, Director of Investor Relations for U.S. Bancorp.

passages.heading: Brian Mauney, Director of Investor Relations
passages.text: Brian Mauney, Director of Investor Relations: Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. Today, I am joined by our Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, Gunjan Kedia, and Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer, John C. Stern. In a moment, Gunjan and John will be referencing a slide presentation together with their prepared remarks. A copy of the presentation, our press release, and supplemental analyst schedules can be found on our website at ir.usbank.com. Please note that any forward-looking statements made during today's call are subject to risk and uncertainty. Factors that could materially change our current forward-looking assumptions are described on Page 2 of today's earnings presentation, our press release, and reports on file with the SEC. Following our prepared remarks, Gunjan and John will be happy to take any questions that you have. I will now turn the call over to Gunjan.

passages.heading: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer: Thank you, Brian. Good morning, everyone. Beginning on Slide 3, we delivered another strong quarter, highlighted by record net revenue of approximately $8 billion and diluted earnings per share of $1.34, up approximately 10% from a year ago. Results in the quarter reflect strong execution against our three strategic priorities. Net revenue grew 8.7% year over year. Disciplined productivity drove 240 basis points of positive operating leverage. And in payments, our transformation efforts continue to gain traction, with total payments revenue growing 6.5% year over year. Turning to Slide 4, fees continued to grow nicely and contributed 44% of total revenue again this quarter. Our fee complex is diversified and deepens client relationships, generates attractive returns, and contributes to a more balanced earnings profile. While fee growth does come with higher expenses, productivity initiatives, including from our AI programs, helped improve our efficiency ratio and increased return on average assets year over year. On Slide 5, we spotlight global capital markets, an attractive growth opportunity across a range of economic scenarios. We closed the BTIG acquisition in June, and it contributed $226 million of fee revenue in the third quarter. Our combined businesses are off to a wonderful start and already working very closely together to broaden how we serve our clients. We expect capital markets to grow from 8% to 10% or more

passages.heading: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: of total company revenue over the next three to five years by focusing on three strategies: one, continue to drive robust core organic growth across both franchises, in line with their historical performance; two, deepen wallet share with our clients where we deploy significant balance sheet resources. The addition of BTIG strengthens our ability to serve a broader range of needs and capture greater fee revenue over time; and three, add product capabilities across both platforms. We look forward to sharing more on our capital markets strategy at a conference later this fall and are committed to providing more disclosures in due course as the business becomes a larger part of our revenue mix. With fees and expenses in a healthy place this year, we have increasingly turned our attention to strengthening net interest income and margin. An important lever of this growth is expanding our consumer and small business franchise, which provides a highly attractive source of funding. Slide 6 is a busy chart. It captures our footprint and expansion strategies. We are densifying our branch presence and leveraging client centers that have long supported our national businesses. We are supporting this ground game with targeted brand investments, including through our NFL partnership, and new brand ambassadors such as Fernando Mendoza, Christian McCaffrey, and, most recently, Jessica Alba for our small business segment. Turning to Slide 7, we highlight small business banking. We serve

passages.heading: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: more than 2 million small businesses through a scaled, interconnected platform. That contributes meaningfully to company revenue and is an invaluable source of stable, well-priced deposits. Over the past several years, we have built a unique foundation of banking, payments, and cash management capabilities. This quarter, we launched several major initiatives to expand our reach with small businesses as we onboarded the Amazon co-brand partnership, expanded the Business Essentials suite of products, and established new banking teams in expansion markets. We have a truly differentiated set of products and an enviable client footprint with small business. And this segment will be an important priority going into 2027. Finally, on Slide 8, I want to spend a moment on corporate payments and treasury management, which together represent approximately 6% of our company revenues. The corporate payments landscape has the potential to be transformed by the growing convergence of treasury management rails like ACH and wires, card rails, and new stablecoins and tokenized deposits. These businesses have delivered a strong quarter, benefiting from market share gains as well as tailwinds from fuel price increases in our fleet and freight businesses. Earlier this quarter, we launched our first USDBC stablecoin pilot. While these trends are emerging, we are uniquely positioned in corporate payments, and we are investing to create interoperability across these rails to deliver both the

passages.heading: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: benefits of new technologies and the safety and soundness of the banking system. Let me now turn it over to John.

passages.heading: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer: Thanks, Gunjan, and good morning, everyone. Third quarter results reflected another strong quarter and demonstrated continued progress against our strategic priorities, generating meaningful revenue growth and significant positive operating leverage. Results remained firmly within all of our medium-term target ranges. If you turn to Slide 9, we provide highlights for the third quarter. We reported earnings per common share of $1.34, with approximately a $0.07 impact from reserve build this quarter. This equates to 10% year-over-year EPS growth, or 16% excluding the reserve build. Revenue was a record $8 billion, up 8.7% from a year ago, or up 6.4% adjusting for BTIG and securities losses. Meanwhile, expenses grew 7.1% year over year, or 2.0% excluding BTIG, implying 440 basis points of positive operating leverage excluding BTIG. Balance sheet trends remain constructive. Loans grew 1.0% and deposits grew 2.2% sequentially, while the net interest margin expanded 5 basis points to 2.84%. Credit quality metrics remained healthy across the board. Linked-quarter nonperforming assets declined 1.6%, and net charge-offs declined 2 basis points to 51 basis points. The CET1 ratio remained stable at 10.8%, and tangible book value per share was up 5.4% year over year. Slide 10 provides our key performance metrics. Our profitability metrics continued to move up and to the right, while our efficiency ratio improved toward the better

passages.heading: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: end of our medium-term target range. Slide 11 provides a summary of our loan and earning asset mix evolution. Average loans grew 8.0% year over year and 1.0% sequentially. Versus the prior year, growth continues to be driven by C&I, credit card, and commercial real estate, categories that typically deepen relationships and deliver incremental fee opportunities. The Amazon small business credit card portfolio contributed approximately $900 million and $1.7 billion to the third-quarter average and period-end loans, respectively. Importantly, our focus in these loan growth areas is naturally positioning our balance sheet to become more asset-sensitive. For example, floating-rate loans comprise 30% of earning assets as of quarter end, up from 22% four years ago. Slide 12 provides a summary of our deposits and funding mix. Total average deposits grew 2.9% year over year and 2.2% sequentially. Growth was driven by another record quarter of consumer deposits, along with strong growth in relationship-based deposits in businesses like investment services. Importantly, we achieved growth while staying disciplined with respect to pricing. Deposit costs increased 7 basis points sequentially, with approximately 2 basis points of impact from the September Fed rate hike. Notably, our total funding costs are up just 1 basis point quarter over quarter as our funding mix continues to improve. Turning to Slide 13, net interest income on a fully taxable-equivalent basis increased 5.6% year

passages.heading: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: over year and 2.3% linked quarter. The increase was driven by continued relationship-based loan and deposit growth, improving earning asset and funding mix, and ongoing benefits from fixed asset repricing. Net interest margin improved 5 basis points sequentially to 2.84%, driven by improving loan yields and fixed asset repricing benefits. We currently expect net interest margin to increase by a similar amount in the fourth quarter. Slide 14 highlights fee revenue trends within noninterest income. Total fee income increased 14.9% year over year, with broad-based strength across most fee categories. Capital markets growth of 69% year over year reflects a full-quarter contribution from BTIG and 10% growth across legacy capital markets. Moving to Slide 15, noninterest expense increased 7.1% versus the prior year, reflecting BTIG and continued investment in growth initiatives, marketing, technology, as well as compensation associated with the strong revenue generation for this quarter. These increases were partially offset by ongoing expense discipline across the bank. Slide 16 highlights the broad-based favorable trends we are seeing in credit quality. On the right side of the page, we highlight the longer-term evolution of our credit card portfolio. Card balances have increased at a brisk pace in recent years as our payments transformation takes hold. At the same time, FICO bands have marginally improved, and net charge-offs and delinquencies have trended lower. In short, we

passages.heading: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: are growing the portfolio without compromising on underwriting standards. Turning to capital on Slide 17, as of September 30, our common equity tier 1 capital ratio was 10.8%, stable compared to the prior quarter. Adjusting for AOCI, the CET1 ratio declined 30 basis points to 9.1%. On Slide 18, we break out the components that drove the sequential changes in the AOCI-adjusted CET1 and tangible common equity ratios this quarter. As it pertains to the adjusted CET1 ratio, strong earnings generation, net of dividends, added approximately 30 basis points of capital. This was offset by $12 billion of risk-weighted asset growth associated with heavy loan demand in the quarter and impact from our recently onboarded strategic small business partnership. Additionally, the significant increase in Treasury rates and widening credit spreads during the third quarter impacted the ratio by an additional 40 basis points. Conversely, the tangible common equity ratio remained stable at 6.6% at quarter end. Strong earnings growth and lower ending assets offset the AOCI drag from higher rates. Despite a sharp move in rates this quarter, we maintained healthy capital levels and continue to have flexibility in how we manage the balance sheet. We expect our capital ratios to build from here, positioning us to resume share repurchases over the next quarter or two. Turning to forward-looking guidance on Slide 19 for the fourth quarter and full year 2026. For the fourth quarter, on a year-over-year

passages.heading: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: basis, we expect net interest income growth of 6% to 7% on a fully taxable-equivalent basis, total fee revenue growth in the range of 13% to 14%, with roughly half of the growth coming from BTIG, and noninterest expense growth of approximately 8%, or closer to 4% excluding BTIG. For full year 2026, we now expect total net revenue growth of 8% to 9% compared to the prior year, or 6% to 7% excluding BTIG. This is improved from our prior guidance range of 5% to 7%. We now expect to deliver approximately 300 basis points of positive operating leverage for the full year, or approximately 400 basis points excluding the impact from BTIG. This is up from prior guidance of 200 and 300 basis points, respectively. Moving to Slide 20, this was another strong quarter for us, reflecting continued execution comfortably within all of our medium-term target ranges. We continue to see momentum across our business, which gives us confidence in our ability to build on these results and deliver consistent, sustainable returns over time. Let me now hand it back to Gunjan for closing remarks.

passages.heading: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer: Thank you, John. As we look to the end of 2026, we are executing well against the strategic priorities we outlined at the beginning of the year and seeing that progress translate into stronger performance across the bank. Our diversified business mix, customer-centric approach, and disciplined execution position us to deliver attractive returns and long-term shareholder value. With that, we will now open the call for your questions.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: At this time, as a reminder, if you would like to ask a question, please press star then 1. Your first question comes from the line of John McDonald from Truist Securities. Your line is open.

passages.heading: John McDonald, Analyst
passages.text: John McDonald, Analyst: Thank you. Good morning. Gunjan mentioned the increased focus on growing net interest income and strengthening the margin. John, could you unpack some of the drivers of your NII outlook from here, including what you see ahead for loan growth and deposit trends?

passages.heading: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer: Sure. Good morning, John. You know, we are going to see similar themes in the fourth quarter that we just saw in the third quarter. Loans have been strong, and they remain strong from a pipeline standpoint. So we expect similar-type growth there. Of course, as a reminder, included in that, we have the Amazon small card book, where we get the full-quarter impact as well. Deposits are performing well. We continue to see nice growth in our consumer franchise as well as small business, and we see continued trends there. And then, in terms of the net interest margin, we made the comment that margin should increase by a similar amount this quarter, and that is going to be aided by the funding and asset mix that we have. That is improving, as we have been talking about. So, you know, there is a lot of momentum that we have, and that is reflected in our guide and what we discussed.

passages.heading: John McDonald, Analyst
passages.text: John McDonald, Analyst: And just to follow up on that, in terms of the net interest margin drivers, could you give us a little feel for how rising rates impact it? Maybe an update on fixed asset repricing and your deposit beta assumptions?

passages.heading: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer: Sure. So, you know, we aim to be as neutral as we can be from an interest rate perspective. However, given this environment, we have been shifting more into asset sensitivity, and you are starting to see that come through in terms of loans. We have been shifting more into C&I, commercial real estate, and card, all predominantly floating-rate assets, as you know. And then in the investment portfolio, that has been coming down, and we have been doing more in cash, so we have been shifting there a bit. In terms of fixed asset repricing, I would say that we continue to see about $10 billion or so per quarter of fixed-rate assets that reprice, whether that is in the securities book or in the loan book, and that is coming on probably at about a 125-basis-point improvement or so. And that has improved a little bit because of the backup in rates that we have seen. And then finally, you asked about deposit betas. You know, we think that betas pick up right where they left off from the last rate hike, so we are assuming about a 50% or so deposit beta to start out with, and likely to continue as we see a couple of hikes coming up in our forecast. So those are kind of the main points.

passages.heading: John McDonald, Analyst
passages.text: John McDonald, Analyst: Got it. Thanks, John.

passages.heading: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer: Thank you.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Scott Siefers from TD Cowen. Your line is open.

passages.heading: Scott Siefers, Analyst
passages.text: Scott Siefers, Analyst: Good morning, guys. Thank you for taking my—yep. Hey. I guess the first one, just sort of a top-level one. You know, it has ended up being a much better year. I think we knew it was going to be a good year from the standpoint of positive operating leverage. It looks like it is coming in even better than expected. I guess as you think about things looking ahead, maybe just sort of top-level thoughts on the balance between profitability improvement and investment—just sort of top-level, how you are thinking about those things?

passages.heading: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer: Yes, sure, Scott. Yes, I mean, our seat—our results—had strong growth in revenue, and that has been gaining momentum as the year has gone on. And so that is going to be the fundamental driver for why the increase in operating leverage this year is from that 200 basis points now up to 300 basis points. We have obviously been onboarding a lot of revenue, with the Amazon card book and BTIG coming online. That is north of $1 billion of revenue we have onboarded. And we signaled this at the beginning of the year. We said that operating leverage, we wanted to be more of a driver from revenue growth because we know we can manage the expense side. We have a lot of levers to do that. So, you know, as we look forward, we are early in the budget process, so we are not giving any guidance, but we anticipate operating leverage next year, given similar drivers that we are seeing this year.

passages.heading: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer: And, Scott, I would just add that we have runway on productivity initiatives. As you know, we have materially invested in our digital capabilities over five years, and that just delivers ongoing productivity. And we continue to be very intentional about how much we spend on technology investments. All in all, I would say it is not a trade-off. We do not think about operating leverage for shareholders or investing into the business. The business model is capable of generating both of them in balance.

passages.heading: Scott Siefers, Analyst
passages.text: Scott Siefers, Analyst: Okay. Thank you for that color. And then, John, just maybe on the repurchase comments. I mean, there has been a lot of focus following just the pause that you disclosed a month or so ago. It sounds like you will restart either this quarter or next quarter. Maybe just thoughts on the main factors you are thinking of as you anticipate returning to repurchase, and maybe just sort of the balance between common equity tier 1 build, TCE considerations, et cetera?

passages.heading: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer: Sure. Yeah. So maybe just to recap, the third quarter had a lot of unique events in it for us. We had strong loan growth. We obviously had the Amazon book that added some capital demands. And then the large rate move, which we all saw, of course. But, you know, for us, given our unique position and just our prudent nature, we decided to pause. But we have a high degree of confidence in our ability to generate capital. I mean, this quarter, after dividend distribution, we generated 33 basis points of capital. So we know we can build that back very quickly. I would just say what we are looking for this quarter is loan demand—where does that actually end up shaking out? Obviously, we believe that there will be growth, as I mentioned in a previous comment. But interest rates, we are watching that very closely. And then, obviously, you have the added component of regulation. We anticipate some new rules coming down. So the combination of all that will be the driver of whether it is this quarter or next. But in the meantime, we are obviously very much committed to the 70% to 75% payout from a capital distribution standpoint.

passages.heading: Scott Siefers, Analyst
passages.text: Scott Siefers, Analyst: Okay. All right. Thank you. Thank you.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Manan Gosalia from Morgan Stanley.

passages.heading: Manan Gosalia, Analyst
passages.text: Manan Gosalia, Analyst: Wanted to ask on commercial loan balances. The average loan balances were essentially flat sequentially, and I think utilization rates declined slightly. Can you talk about what you are seeing in terms of underlying corporate borrowing demand, given that rates were expected to go up and most of your clients are on the short end of the curve? Is there some reduction in demand overall? Or, in terms of the slowdown this quarter, was any of that related to capital levels and the ability to deploy capital, given the shift in the long end of the curve?

passages.heading: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer: Sure. Thanks, Manan. You know, what I would say is that the underlying core C&I growth is very healthy and strong. We did have some runoff in some balances related more to that NDFI space. And some of this is just new deals coming to market that did not hurdle our areas, and we have been more thoughtful on that of late. And so that is really the reason that you see the C&I component being pretty flat on a linked-quarter basis. We do anticipate that to increase as we look into the fourth quarter. So the pipelines remain robust, and it is in all the areas that we have talked about in terms of food and beverage, energy, and technology. Those are obviously very strong areas of loan demand at this point. So those are kind of the core things I would say on the C&I line.

passages.heading: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer: No, I would add that the only place we have seen a little slowdown is commercial real estate and residential mortgage. It continues to be very muted. But otherwise, C&I loan demand is quite robust and broad-based.

passages.heading: Manan Gosalia, Analyst
passages.text: Manan Gosalia, Analyst: Got it. And can you unpack those comments you just made on the capital side a little bit more? You mentioned the regulators changing the endgame rules and how that might give you some flexibility. So I guess you are saying that if the 10-year stays where it is, plus you get some more color from the regulators on which way they are taking it, that you can start buybacks as soon as the fourth quarter?

passages.heading: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer: Yes. I mean, that is a component. Obviously, we are all for Basel III endgame. We have signaled that is about a 5% or so improvement to the RWA, but that is from the proposal. Things can change, so we need to see that. The tailoring comments have been in the news, and so we are watching to see if anything comes online in that regard. So those are incremental pieces of information. But also, it is going to be rates and RWA slash loan growth. Those are the three main components. And we will clearly update you. But it is clear we will be starting that back up, and we will glide back up into that 70% to 75%, as we just mentioned. We have a high degree of confidence in our capital build.

passages.heading: Manan Gosalia, Analyst
passages.text: Manan Gosalia, Analyst: Okay. Thank you. Thanks.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Ebrahim Poonawala from Bank of America. Your line is open.

passages.heading: Ebrahim Poonawala, Analyst
passages.text: Ebrahim Poonawala, Analyst: Hey. Good morning. Good morning. I guess maybe this is the first question. On Slide 6, where you have the national footprint, just talk to us in terms of what the strategy around the client centers is. Obviously, you have seen many of your peers announce significant branch expansion in new markets. Is this a precursor to adding a ton of branches, or is this an indication that you do not see a ton of value in adding hundreds of branches and the client centers allow you to achieve the same outcomes and reach? Would love your strategic thought process behind that.

passages.heading: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer: Good morning, Ebrahim. So I will just start by saying we do see value in branches, and we do see them as anchoring very high-quality customer relationships. Just to back up a little bit, we had been on a journey for really a decade to transform our branch network from what used to be a lot of small tier-three service outlets to more advice hubs with most of our products being there. That was the renovation strategy. That is finishing up now, and we are beginning to lean into new branches. We have shared that our branch investment has increased from $200 million or thereabouts on average to $300 million, which is what we expect to do going forward. And those will be more new branches. Our first phase of that work is to densify within our own footprint. As you see from the blue dots, we are in a vast territory, and we have a real, meaningful opportunity to get to 8% to 10% branch share in those markets within our footprint that have high household formation rates. There, our brand is already known, our operations are already established, and the return is very high. It is fully our expectation that over time, we will inch out from that footprint to other branches. The client centers, on the other hand, are an interim answer that is fast for us to establish national presence. This is not a new strategy. Our commercial teams, our wealth teams, our mortgage teams, and our commercial real estate teams have been operating out of a

passages.heading: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: footprint. The Northeast is the big site for capital markets-type businesses as well. And what we have done more recently is to say small business can also operate out of client centers. So the strategy is both, and it is a matter of sequencing.

passages.heading: Ebrahim Poonawala, Analyst
passages.text: Ebrahim Poonawala, Analyst: Got it. So I guess it is safe to say over time those red dots, which feel quite lonely, will get accompanied by more blue dots, I guess.

passages.heading: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer: We hope to make them less lonely, Ebrahim. Yes.

passages.heading: Ebrahim Poonawala, Analyst
passages.text: Ebrahim Poonawala, Analyst: Thank you. Understood. And just one separate question on the broad-based C&I growth. Obviously, even in the last week, your markets are once again questioning the AI CapEx buildout. To the extent you have visibility, just talk to us: when you think about broad-based C&I growth, how much of that are you able to see as the second- or third-derivative effect of the data center buildout versus just other industries where we are seeing growth that may be less connected to the AI CapEx cycle? Thank you.

passages.heading: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer: Thanks, Ebrahim. Yeah, it is a topic that comes up frequently for us. We are looking to see if there are clues as to how much growth and credit impact there is related to AI. I mean, obviously, you have adjacent sectors like energy and telecom and things like that, areas that are seeing benefit in loan growth. But then there are other areas that are more broad-based and beyond that, in terms of retail, food and beverage, insurance, and all these other sorts of things. So it is broad-based. And I would actually add on top of that small business with SBA loans and things like that. There is a lot of momentum in the business community to want to grow. So that is on our mindset right now, and we are for that. But it is a topic we certainly look at.

passages.heading: Ebrahim Poonawala, Analyst
passages.text: Ebrahim Poonawala, Analyst: Got it. Thank you.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Your next question comes from the line of John Pancari from Evercore ISI. Your line is open.

passages.heading: John Pancari, Analyst
passages.text: John Pancari, Analyst: Good morning, John. Good morning, John. Good morning. I want to see if you can maybe unpack a little bit of the trends you are seeing within the fee income space, particularly around treasury management, virtual processing, and corporate payments. Just some of the business color that you are seeing in terms of demand, as well as how you look going into 2027 with a good, reasonable pace of growth as you continue to emphasize these businesses. And maybe similar color around the underlying pipeline that you are seeing on the capital markets side.

passages.heading: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer: Sure. So, yeah, a couple of things there. I will start on the treasury management and corporate payments side. Obviously, we saw some very strong growth on that side of the equation. In the corporate payments side, we saw about 19% year-on-year growth. Most of that is new business, as well as spending from corporates and government being up quite a bit from last year. At this time last year, recall, there were impacts of tariffs and all that sort of thing. We have lapped all that, and so there is good growth there. There is a little bit of fuel spend as well in there, but that is pretty nominal in terms of the growth rate. So we do expect continued growth in the CPS, or corporate payments, side of the equation. And the treasury management side is continuing to see nice growth in that mid-single-digit area. It is an important business. We have been making a lot of investments of late, and so we are doing a lot in terms of the payable and digital channels and capabilities. Going forward, we have high hopes in these two areas, for sure. On the capital markets side, we continue to see strong growth into the next quarter. Obviously, we had very strong growth of 69% or so this quarter. BTIG will continue to be a strong component of that at about $200 million or so. But our core FICC, or legacy capital markets, led by commodities, foreign exchange, and impact finance, are really showing some nice growth, and that is going to

passages.heading: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: help us get some more in the double-digit type of growth on a year-over-year basis. So we feel very good about those areas.

passages.heading: John Pancari, Analyst
passages.text: John Pancari, Analyst: Okay. Thanks, John. It is helpful. And then on the margin side, just looking for a little bit more color on what you are seeing in terms of competition. Mike, I heard you on the deposit beta commentary. What are you seeing there on deposit pricing in terms of market trends and how that is influencing your actions on the deposit side? And then similarly, on the loan side, I know you mentioned a little earlier that within the C&I book, a couple of deals did not hurdle. You expect that to pick up. What are you seeing in terms of pressures on spreads and loan pricing on the lending side? Thanks.

passages.heading: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer: Sure. The answer is going to be pretty boring. We are not seeing a whole lot of change on both the deposit and loan side of the equation from a pricing standpoint. Post-hike, the pricing that we are seeing is very consistent with what you would expect. There is nothing out of the ordinary. I would say similar on the loan side. Loan spreads, by and large, tend to be pretty stable. It is competitive, of course, but it is manageable. On the C&I side of the equation, as I just mentioned, some of those things just did not hurdle. Some of that is a little bit more—we have been more prescriptive with the businesses in terms of making sure that things hurdle. And so it is a little bit of a dial turn for us that occurred. But we see broad-based growth in the C&I portfolio.

passages.heading: John Pancari, Analyst
passages.text: John Pancari, Analyst: Okay. Great. Thanks, John.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Ken Usdin from Autonomous Research. Your line is open.

passages.heading: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer: Good morning, Ken.

passages.heading: Ken Usdin, Analyst
passages.text: Ken Usdin, Analyst: Hey. Good morning. Hey, John, can I just ask you to walk through a couple more things on fees? Obviously, the guide implies sequentially lower fees for the fourth quarter, and I know a lot of that is seasonal. Can you just remind us what usually happens in the payment lines? Does capital markets hold up at the third-quarter level? I know you are saying $200 million of BTIG versus $226 million. And then can you size the amount of equity gains that were in the other line and what that line should usually look like?

passages.heading: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer: Sure. Yes. The fourth quarter, from a year-over-year growth standpoint, is going to look a lot like the third quarter, with a couple of exceptions, which explains the slightly lower growth rate, although it is still very, very strong. Mortgages are going to be impacted by higher rates, and so we anticipate there to be more limited or low year-on-year growth, if any. And then other revenue—we did have some gains that were more unique to this quarter. Our other revenue tends to be in the $120 million to $150 million range. So we anticipate that to normalize into that. Other than that, I think things like corporate trust continue to be very strong. I talked about capital markets. Many of the payments lines—we see strong growth in corporate as well as retail cards. Merchant will probably still be in that 0% area for the next couple of quarters, as we have talked about. And all the other areas are about as expected. So it is shaping up to be a lot of momentum for us on the fee side of the equation.

passages.heading: Ken Usdin, Analyst
passages.text: Ken Usdin, Analyst: Okay. Thanks, John. And then secondly, with the NIM up 5 this quarter and you are saying up about the same amount, at the 2.90-ish exit, can you just talk about—I know balance sheet size and mix will be an important part of this answer—but your comments previously about getting to a 3% NIM in 2027. Can you talk about how that looks and what needs to happen in terms of the mix and size of the balance sheet vis-à-vis prior questions on rates and such? Thanks.

passages.heading: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer: Yeah. You know, Ken, we continue to see a path to a 3% NIM at some point in 2027. You are starting to see that thesis play out, as we have talked about. It is a constant formula of consistent asset repricing, as I have just mentioned. The asset and funding mix is continuing to improve, and then we are just being thoughtful in terms of deposit acquisition versus cost. Those are the formula and the ingredients that we need to continue to do what we are doing on the NIM side. Obviously, the curve and deposit competition may have something to say about that in the end, but we have a lot to like in terms of the trajectory we are making on that path. So we feel good about it.

passages.heading: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer: You know, I will add one thing: we are very disciplined about improving both the deposit mix and the loan mix, which is helping the NIM. For the fourth quarter, we have the full-year impact of the Amazon deal, which is a nice tailwind. But we are continuing to focus on credit card receivables, which are growing very well, and on C&I loans and CRE. As that becomes a bigger part of our loan book and deposits become more relationship-oriented, it gives us strengthening NIM and NII growth for some time.

passages.heading: Ken Usdin, Analyst
passages.text: Ken Usdin, Analyst: I got it. Thank you very much.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Chris McGratty from KBW. Your line is open.

passages.heading: Chris McGratty, Analyst
passages.text: Chris McGratty, Analyst: Maybe a question on credit. In the higher-rate environment, any comments from the team on the impact you have seen so far on consumers? And also the health of the commercial customer? I know you talked about moving some of the NDFI lending out in the quarter.

passages.heading: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer: Sure. On the credit side, we have not really seen a whole lot of change. It is obviously a watch item when we think about the impacts of higher rates. Right now, we are not seeing anything on the consumer side. Spend levels are high. Employment is strong. So there continue to be strong patterns there, despite sentiment and things of that variety. And then on the commercial side, corporates and commercial clients are well-managed. They have strong balance sheets. They have been going through a lot over the last several years, and they have been very nimble. I think the area we are watching, obviously, is going to be commercial real estate. You always want to watch when rates go up. And obviously, when we underwrite, we build in cushion for rate moves. So it is well understood and managed, but it is going to be an area that we watch. Nothing at this point to call out.

passages.heading: Chris McGratty, Analyst
passages.text: Chris McGratty, Analyst: Okay. Thanks, John. And I think I may have asked this in prior quarters, but just in the broader balance sheet optimization discussion today, with where rates have moved and the growth that has occurred, is there anything additionally that might be ripe for optimization, whether it be the funding base, perhaps syndicating more production into the capital markets for a quarter or two? Anything we should be aware of there?

passages.heading: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer: Yeah. You know, I think we are doing the actions, and we will just continue action from us. In this environment, you want to be very active in your management of the balance sheet, and I have already mentioned several of those things that we have done. Maybe some other things you have probably noticed: our long-term debt fell a couple billion dollars as the investment portfolio—we did repay some Federal Home Loan Bank advances that were long-term debt, but there was not much maturity left in them. So we are just being active. As I mentioned, we have been lowering the amount in the investment portfolio and going more into cash. We are doing a lot of things to optimize the balance sheet for the rate environment that we are entering, and we feel good about taking action as needed.

passages.heading: Chris McGratty, Analyst
passages.text: Chris McGratty, Analyst: Great. Thanks, John.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Gerard Cassidy from RBC. Your line is open.

passages.heading: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer: Good morning, Gerard.

passages.heading: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer: Good morning, Gerard.

passages.heading: Gerard Cassidy, Analyst
passages.text: Gerard Cassidy, Analyst: Hey, John. Back in your Investor Day, Gunjan, I guess it was the fall of 2024, you talked a lot about interconnectedness. And when you look at your Slide 5 on BTIG, you talk about deepening the client base. Can you share with us how that opportunity for cross-selling into your existing client base for BTIG products, and vice versa, is proceeding? What are the opportunities that you see for growing that business through that interconnectedness?

passages.heading: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer: Thank you, Gerard. It has actually gone very well. As you know, when we did the BTIG deal, the biggest questions were around cultural fit. The chemistry is very good, and the substantive ability to deepen relationships is very good. As you know, we deploy a very significant balance sheet to our corporate relationships. Having more products to get your fair share of fee revenue is an important part of the interconnected piece, and it is coming through very nicely. It has also been very encouraging to see it on the other side. We have developed a very sizable relationship book in leveraged ETFs, and a lot of the trading opportunity that comes from that helps BTIG, too. So we expect that this will be a very good deal for us, and we are very confident in getting the combined capital markets business to about 10% of total net revenue or more over time. And that completes the product set. I will also answer a broader question on interconnectivity: it is really playing out with deposits right now. There is a lot of discussion around deposit cost, deposit betas, and the Smartly product that we launched about two years back, around the time of Investor Day. It connects our banking products to our credit card products and allows a person to optimize their card rewards based on their deposited deposit relationships. That product has been very successful for us. You have seen the funding mix improvements based on that. And that is

passages.heading: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: exactly the thesis we are taking now to small business. So this theme of interconnecting is very present in the company. It takes incentive changes, some changes to org structures, and some development of skill sets. But we have had a lot of momentum there and it will continue to be a very big part of our strategy even into next year.

passages.heading: Gerard Cassidy, Analyst
passages.text: Gerard Cassidy, Analyst: Very good. And then as a follow-up, obviously, maybe you can update us since you have been very active in doing some bolt-on acquisitions, just as BTIG, for example, as well as the portfolio acquisition. Where are you standing now in terms of either more bolt-on acquisitions as you look out into the future, or possibly even a depository acquisition? Thank you.

passages.heading: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer: Sure. Our point of view remains consistent. We like bolt-on acquisitions. We are good at it, and they give us local scale and products. We do not think of them as fundamentally different from investing organically into our business. On depository acquisition, we find our organic strategies to have compelling strategic, financial, and execution merits, and we are very, very focused on that part of the strategy and have a lot of momentum there.

passages.heading: Gerard Cassidy, Analyst
passages.text: Gerard Cassidy, Analyst: Appreciate it. Thank you, Gunjan.

passages.heading: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer: Thank you.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Mike Mayo from Wells Fargo. Your line is open.

passages.heading: Mike Mayo, Analyst
passages.text: Mike Mayo, Analyst: Hi. You increased your guide for operating leverage this year by 100 basis points, and I think you said one reason was related to AI. That is a little surprising because it is hard for banks to actually quantify benefits, and banks usually talk about AI benefits in more general terms like productivity and stuff like that. So were you talking in a more general sense, or do you have numbers around it? How are you using AI, and why do you think it is helping to improve your efficiency? Thank you.

passages.heading: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer: Good morning, Mike. So I think AI is one, not the only, reason to drive good productivity, but it is an important lever and has growing momentum and growing use cases for productivity within our world. We do continue to expect it to be a contributor to productivity. Some of the discussions around whether the token costs are overtaking returns are relevant. We have invested in developing the capabilities to swap out models for cheaper models, and we have some confidence that over time we will continue to get positive returns from our AI program on productivity. More broadly, though, the place where we are being more measured is on client-facing applications, as we fully understand the concerns around privacy and some of the customer confidence issues around it. These things will get resolved in due course. So we remain quite focused on the AI program and do have confidence around its contribution to our productivity.

passages.heading: Mike Mayo, Analyst
passages.text: Mike Mayo, Analyst: And as it relates to the cash-sorting concerns—that AI agents will drain deposits from the banking industry—how do you think about that potential threat and the value that U.S. Bancorp provides to depositors, say, for privacy and trust? Thank you.

passages.heading: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer: So, Mike, first, we have not seen any AI cash-sorting third-party agents try to interact with the bank. The logistics of doing something like this are very complicated, so we do not expect it to be a near-term impact to us. Our customer base is very digitally savvy. The adoption rates are very high. Our tools allow a fairly high amount of deposit price discovery and the ability to optimize automatically should a depositor choose to do that. All of these capabilities will strengthen with AI over time. We are not counting on it not to be that way. But, again, our strategy is not to attract depositors only through deposit price. We have invested a lot in creating meaningful value propositions that help people manage their lives and manage their transactions, and we are quite comfortable with transparency around deposit pricing. So I would say there is a lot of discussion around that topic. We do not see it yet in day-to-day life.

passages.heading: Mike Mayo, Analyst
passages.text: Mike Mayo, Analyst: All right. Thank you.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Erika Najarian from UBS. Your line is open.

passages.heading: Erika Najarian, Analyst
passages.text: Erika Najarian, Analyst: Hi, good morning. I had a few follow-up questions.

passages.heading: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer: Good morning.

passages.heading: Erika Najarian, Analyst
passages.text: Erika Najarian, Analyst: Going back to the exit rate on the net interest margin, I just wanted to drill down on this given Gunjan's remarks about focusing on strengthening NII. John, in the past, you have mentioned that you are liability-sensitive to the short end. As we think about the path from the fourth quarter to that 3%, is the optimization on the funding side and the asset remix enough to offset that sort of initial liability sensitivity, assuming the curve flattens from the rate hikes? In other words, does that balance sheet optimization overwhelm that static positioning on the short end?

passages.heading: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer: Sure. So, on the mix and all this sort of thing, we have continued to—and want to—improve our asset mix to be more floating rate. That has been an area that we have talked about here and even put a slide in to show how much we have moved over the last couple of years and been methodical about that. So the answer is yes. We think the funding and asset mix and the fixed asset repricing are enough to offset any competition on the beta side. That is what we are developing on the balance sheet side of the equation, and that is what gives us confidence, as I mentioned, in terms of the NIM path and all that sort of thing. Obviously, we will watch the curve shape and what that looks like and how the deposit competition fans out, but that is what our assumptions are at this particular juncture.

passages.heading: Erika Najarian, Analyst
passages.text: Erika Najarian, Analyst: Got it. And just a follow-up question. You are certainly in a unique position in terms of Category II, and there is a big difference between a cliff vesting of AOCI and a five-year phase-in. We are hearing that Basel III endgame will be finalized by year end, and it just feels like tailoring has to come with it, given the phase-in component. Do you have a sense on whether, if we do get finalization of Basel III endgame, that would be the superseding rule for you versus the cliff vesting on AOCI? In other words, would you get to enjoy a five-year phase-in versus the cliff vesting? If so, does that change anything in terms of how you are thinking about buybacks from either a timing or magnitude perspective?

passages.heading: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer: Yeah. I will go back to my comments that we are certainly looking at regulation as a component of deciding on buybacks. But it is going to be probably more dependent on RWA demands as well as interest rates, particularly in the short run. We are very much interested in rule changes that we expect to see here in the fourth quarter. That can shift what our ultimate RWA and capital demands are or what they look like. We are also interested, obviously, if there is tailoring and how that gets applied. It is speculation at this point, right? We know just as much as you do from what we see in the press. But we are not planning on it. We are planning on growing our capital base and on all the things that we talked about in terms of balance sheet stewardship and optimization. Those are going to help us on our path. But that is it.

passages.heading: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer: I just want to double underline that. We are fully ready to transition into Category II regardless of the timing of the Basel III endgame. We have been preparing for it for a long time. And when John talks about starting share repurchases in the next one or two quarters, we are not counting on any benefit from Basel III endgame. This is just capital accretion we get based on normal-course business.

passages.heading: Erika Najarian, Analyst
passages.text: Erika Najarian, Analyst: Got it. Thank you so much.

passages.heading: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer: Thanks, Erika.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Ken Usdin from Citi. Your line is open.

passages.heading: Analyst, Analyst
passages.text: Analyst, Analyst: Hi, good morning. Good morning. It is helpful to hear the thoughts on overall growth and then kind of bolt-on opportunities if they do arise, if you do go that route. Just thinking about the loan portfolio itself: you have had some organic growth, and you have had some remixing with the card. Just thinking, not necessarily as a fourth-quarter comment or even a 2027 comment, but down the road, how should we think about the relative mix and weighting between some of the loan categories, and the areas that you would see as more appealing today?

passages.heading: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer: Sure, Ken. I can start on that. I think what you have been seeing on the loan side of the equation, you will continue to see over the past several quarters and for the next several quarters, in terms of leaning in on card, leaning in on C&I, and commercial real estate. Now there may be some bumps—for example, commercial real estate may not be as robust in the next quarter or two, just given the backup in rates. But all in, we are focusing in that way. When we started the year, I believe our residential mortgage loans were in the 30% area in terms of loan mix. We do see that coming down, more because the other categories are growing into it. So we anticipate the mortgage area will probably be in the mid-twenties at some point over time. But, again, it is going to be because of the growth in the other areas, not because we are diminishing our focus on the residential mortgage book. We continue to think that is a strong business over the fullness of time.

passages.heading: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer: Our thought process very much is that it is a relationship loan. Where you get fee revenue, deep relationships, and sticky deposits, that is where we want to extend our balance sheet. The categories that lend themselves to this are credit cards—it is a big fee-based business—and C&I loans, where our corporate payments and investment services products make that a very attractive loan. And as we build out the capital markets, that becomes a good use of balance sheet as well. The categories that we would be more measured on would include auto, mortgage, and some of these more standalone products, which will still be very important products for us over time. But, as John said, we will just be more measured.

passages.heading: Analyst, Analyst
passages.text: Analyst, Analyst: Got it. That is helpful. Thank you.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: Your next question comes from the line of David Chiaverini from Jefferies. Your line is open.

passages.heading: David Chiaverini, Analyst
passages.text: David Chiaverini, Analyst: Thanks for taking the question. Wanted to ask about the efficiency ratio outlook. Your guide is mid-to-high 50s. What could take U.S. Bancorp to the high end versus the low end? And to what extent does the interest rate environment influence that?

passages.heading: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer
passages.text: John C. Stern, Vice Chair and Chief Financial Officer: Sure. So right now, obviously, we are around 56, just under that, which we are very proud of in terms of making good progress there. The operating leverage has helped with the revenue growth that we have seen. We continue to anticipate strong growth and continuing that operating leverage. Our desire is to get closer to that mid part of the range, versus the mid-to-high 50s. That is an area we are focused on. Obviously, the rate environment and the macro will drive things here and there, but that has been our focus and what we have been talking about.

passages.heading: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer: I would say the high end will be if capital markets growth turns out to be very robust, and that will be a good reason to be on the high end. That is a high-efficiency-ratio business. The low end will be our AI program. There is a lot to be discovered there, a lot of potential, and you can see a path where that accelerates and really begins to impact the productivity of the firm.

passages.heading: David Chiaverini, Analyst
passages.text: David Chiaverini, Analyst: Thanks for that. And then I wanted to ask about USDBC. You mentioned how it launched in September. Did you launch this due to strong client demand, or is this more about getting the capability up and running in anticipation of increased client demand down the road?

passages.heading: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer
passages.text: Gunjan Kedia, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer: It is certainly the latter. I very clearly have to say there is not much client demand at all. What there is now is client curiosity. Even from two quarters back, we have quite a few clients wanting to experiment with us on what this might do. The launch, as you know, is a pilot. The launch of the product will take some regulatory approvals. We do think that as companies think about combining the benefits of the banking system, which they really do like and appreciate, with some of the shortcomings—mostly what we have heard is 24/7 real-time availability, especially over the weekends, and cross-border, where most central banks do not have that kind of capability—we are building out the product set in anticipation of being able to do something that creates value for customers. But we would not say that there is very robust demand that has developed just yet. Most of the conversations are around the corporate payment space. Thank you.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: And there are no further questions at this time. Mr. Mauney, I turn the call back over to you.

passages.heading: Brian Mauney, Director of Investor Relations
passages.text: Brian Mauney, Director of Investor Relations: Yes. Thank you to everyone who joined our call this morning. Please contact the Investor Relations department if you have any follow-up questions. Robert, you may now disconnect.

passages.heading: Operator, Operator
passages.text: Operator, Operator: This concludes today's conference call. You may now disconnect.
